stories.title: Sagehall Picks Up Chetrit Organization’s 428 Broadway for $47M
stories.excerpt: An entity linked to New York City-based private real estate investment firm Sagehall has purchased Chetrit Organization’s office building at 428 Broadway for $47 million, according to city records filed Thursday. Jason Levine, managing director at Sagehall, signed for the buyer entity, 428 Broadway Owner. The seller entities are a partnership between the Chetrit Organization, for which Michael Chetrit signed on behalf of two holding companies, and investor American Industrial, co-founded by Roget Lerner and Jean-Marc Donics, the latter of whom signed on behalf of entity AI SoHo Investors. Chetrit Group purchased the six-story property in Manhattan’s SoHo neighborhood in 2005 for $22.5 million. It became the property of the Chetrit Organization in the years following the family’s enterprise split in the mid-2000s. The building eventually ran into distress after its four-floor anchor tenant, WeWork, filed for bankruptcy in 2023. The coworking firm’s departure from 428 Broadway left the building 96 percent vacant. Its current level of occupancy is unclear. Lender LoanCore Capital Credit began foreclosure actions against 428 Broadway in 2024, alongside 1 Whitehall Street in the Financial District, claiming default on roughly $200 million worth of loans. The latter office building was sold earlier this year for $105 million to Nathan Berman’s Metro Loft and Idan Ofer’s Quantum Pacific Group for a planned residential conversion. The mortgage debt on 428 Broadway appears to have changed hands from LoanCore to an entity belonging to Chetrit Organization and Donics, C&AI Soho Holding, in late 2025. The entity took ownership of the property in a recent foreclosure auction, allowing the partners to facilitate a sale. Donic declined to comment on the recent sale, while spokespeople for Sagehall and Chetrit did not immediately respond to requests for comment. bullets: Sagehall acquires distressed 428 Broadway, Manhattan SoHo office for $47M after WeWork bankruptcy left 96% vacant.
Property purchased 2005 for $22.5M; distress follows anchor tenant WeWork filing 2023, significant value destruction.
Office conversion or redevelopment signal; SoHo office-to-residential conversion remains challenging given zoning, structural constraints.
stories.summary: Sagehall acquired the six-story office building at 428 Broadway in SoHo for $47 million, down from the Chetrit Organization's 2005 purchase price of $22.5 million. The property fell into distress after WeWork, a four-floor anchor tenant, filed for bankruptcy in 2023, leaving the building 96 percent vacant. The transaction suggests either a conversion play, repositioning into life sciences or tech office, or ground-up redevelopment.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily demand signal. However, persistent office distress in Manhattan's premium neighborhoods (SoHo) may unlock conversion opportunities if zoning permits; conversely, it signals weak office-to-residential arbitrage in tight SoHo lots. Developers should monitor whether Sagehall pursues adaptive reuse—if feasible, it could unlock pent-up residential demand in high-barrier-to-entry neighborhoods, but execution risk and capital intensity are high.

stories.title: Panelists from Connect Texas Multifamily Discuss Where We Are in “The Cycle”
stories.excerpt: The apartment investor, developer and renter are all affected by cycles endemic in the industry. Where are we now? A handful of panelists at the Connect Texas Multifamily conference at The Joule weighed in on where we are when it comes to cycles. Greg Willett from Leaseback believes we just crested, “Midyear was the pivot point. We are now starting to see demand exceeding the delivery volume. As deliveries have slowed a bit, we’ve had some rent growth at the top of the market. The signal of recovery is happening now.” Affinius Capital’s Hailey Ghalib added, “We’re transitioning from this significant supply and demand cycle into the recovery. Supply will keep declining until at least 2028, 29.” Jason Houn from ZOM Living sees a change in offering concessions, “Due to the supply, mini-markets outside Austin have had to give concessions up to 12 weeks, such as in Hutto and Pflugerville. But in Austin, it’s dipped to 8 weeks.” And he sees it dipping further. And not all are treated equally in a cycle. Rob Waltz from Trimont says, while things may be improving in the Class A and B+ project, he’s not seeing the turnaround in the B- and C Class apartments, “Those are suffering. Owners of that class of apartments are capped on what renters are able to pay, and yet expenses keep going up.” The post Panelists from Connect Texas Multifamily Discuss Where We Are in “The Cycle” appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Austin-area rent growth signal; Leaseback analyst reports midyear 2024 pivot, demand now exceeds delivery.
Concessions declining: Austin Class A/B+ at 8 weeks vs. suburban markets (Hutto, Pflugerville) at 12 weeks.
B- and C-Class apartments suffering; expense growth outpacing rent growth; widening bifurcation by quality tier.
stories.summary: Panelists at Connect Texas Multifamily conference reported the cycle inflection point occurred midyear 2024, with supply growth slowing and demand now exceeding deliveries. Concessions are declining in Austin proper (down to 8 weeks from prior levels) while suburban mini-markets remain pressured (12-week concessions in Hutto, Pflugerville). However, lower-tier Class B- and C apartments are not recovering; rising expenses continue to compress margins as rents remain capped.
stories.impact: Central Texas multifamily is bifurcating sharply. Developers should prioritize Class A/B+ in Austin core or high-visibility suburban nodes; B- and C-Class conversion or repositioning is economically strained. Supply will remain tight through 2028–29, creating a window for trophy-asset development in Austin proper, but avoid commodity multifamily in secondary rings unless cost of capital improves materially or rents accelerate faster than operating expense inflation.

stories.title: CIM Group, Hulic Pick Up White Plains Apartment Building
stories.excerpt: CIM Group has made its first foray into Westchester County by acquiring a new 135-unit apartment building in White Plains, NY, in partnership with Japan’s Hulic Co., Ltd. Although financial terms were not disclosed, the Westfair Business Journal reported that the asset sold for $64.3 million. Located at 51 S. Broadway, the property was completed in 2025 by Connecticut-based developer RMS Cos. The eight-story building, dubbed 51 South, features contemporary studio, one- and two-bedroom apartments, along with more than 20,000 feet of amenities including a coworking space and indoor and outdoor lounges. “We believe the market benefits from strong fundamentals, connectivity to New York City, and continued demand for quality housing,” said Shaul Kuba, Co-Founder and Principal, CIM Group in a statement. CIM Group has delivered more than $60 billion of real estate and infrastructure projects across the Americas. The company previously partnered with Hulic on the purchase of a 166-unit apartment community in West Hollywood, CA this past July. The post CIM Group, Hulic Pick Up White Plains Apartment Building appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: CIM Group, Hulic acquire 135-unit 51 South in White Plains, NY completed 2025 for ~$64.3M.
First Westchester County entry for CIM; signals capital repositioning into suburban NYC transit nodes.
White Plains demand drivers: NYC connectivity, quality housing shortage; repeat CIM-Hulic partnership (West Hollywood in July 2024).
stories.summary: CIM Group and Japan-based Hulic Co. acquired the newly completed 51 South, a 135-unit, eight-story apartment building in White Plains, NY for approximately $64.3 million. The property features studio, one-, and two-bedroom units plus 20,000+ sq. ft. of amenities including coworking space. This marks CIM's first Westchester County investment and their second partnership with Hulic in under a year.
stories.impact: Signals institutional capital flowing into suburban NYC transit-oriented markets as alternative to saturated Manhattan/Brooklyn core. White Plains sits on Metro-North with reliable NYC commute, positioning it for continued rental demand from remote/hybrid workforce seeking lower rents and quality finishes. Developers should prioritize Westchester TOD sites near Metro-North stations (White Plains, New Rochelle, Stamford) and secure entitlements soon; foreign capital (Japan) targeting Northeast suburban yield suggests cap rate compression in these secondary markets may accelerate.

stories.title: Frontier Realty Group Acquires Shopping Center in PA for $76M
stories.excerpt: Frontier Realty Group, a joint venture between Wharton Realty Group and KSR Capital, announced the acquisition of Miracle Mile Shopping Center in Monroeville, Pennsylvania, for $75.5 million. The deal is the first transaction following the recent launch of Frontier’s national shopping center investment platform. To lead its continued expansion, Frontier has appointed industry veteran Robbie Millman as its Head of Acquisitions, overseeing the platform’s investment strategy. The Frontier Realty Group acquisition team included Daniel Massry, Marc Sitt, Robbie Millman, Isaac Massry, Morris Sabbagh, and Abraham Kassin. CBRE’s Colin Behr, Christopher Munley, Ryan Sciullo, and Chris Sicher represented the prior owners in the transaction. Miracle Mile comprises over 302,000 square feet across 27.5 acres in the Pittsburgh MSA. At 100% occupancy, the center’s tenants include Marshalls, LA Fitness, ULTA, Old Navy, Chick-fil-A, Panera Bread, and DSW Shoe Warehouse. Miracle Mile is well-positioned with direct access to major thoroughfares, including Interstate 376 and the Pennsylvania Turnpike. The post Frontier Realty Group Acquires Shopping Center in PA for $76M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Frontier Realty Group (Wharton Realty + KSR Capital) acquires Miracle Mile Shopping Center, Monroeville PA for $75.5M.
302,000 sq. ft., 27.5 acres, 100% occupied; anchors include Marshalls, LA Fitness, ULTA, Chick-fil-A.
Retail investment thesis unrelated to multifamily; no direct demand/supply signal for apartments.
stories.summary: Frontier Realty Group, a joint venture between Wharton Realty Group and KSR Capital, purchased Miracle Mile Shopping Center in Monroeville, Pennsylvania for $75.5 million. The fully leased 302,000-sq.-ft. center on 27.5 acres features national retailers and is positioned on high-traffic corridors (I-376, Pennsylvania Turnpike). This marks the launch of Frontier's national shopping center investment platform.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. Retail real estate and apartment markets operate on separate capital flows and cycles. No secondary demand signal (e.g., population influx, job creation from retail tenants) is evident from this transaction.

stories.title: Miami-Area Warehouse Sells for $21M
stories.excerpt: Terreno Realty has sold a 113,000-square-foot industrial property west of Miami International Airport for $21.3 million, according to a deed made public this week. An affiliate of Dallas-based Dalfen Industrial, owner of a number of warehouses in South Florida, acquired the 3.4-acre industrial property at 7600 Northwest 26th Street, records show. The previous sale price was $12.1 million in 2012. Terreno, a publicly traded company headquartered in Bellevue, Wash., said in a news release that the distribution building is 100 percent leased to one unnamed tenant. AerSale, a seller of airplanes, engines and landing gear, reports on its website that it occupies the space. Terreno said the transaction generated an unleveraged internal rate of return of 11.1 percent. The warehouse was built in 1973, according to property records. Terreno has been an active buyer and seller of Miami industrial space. In 2025, the company paid $196 million for a distribution complex in Doral, Fla. Dalfen Industrial has been an active buyer and seller, too. It owns more than 200 industrial properties nationally. Jeff Ostrowski can be reached at jostrowski@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Dalfen Industrial acquires 113,000 sq. ft. Miami-area warehouse west of airport for $21.3M; 100% leased to AerSale.
Asset price appreciation: $12.1M (2012) to $21.3M (2025); 11.1% unleveraged IRR for Terreno seller.
Miami industrial market remains tight; South Florida warehouse scarcity supports both pricing and leasing velocity.
stories.summary: Terreno Realty sold a 113,000-sq.-ft. industrial property near Miami International Airport to a Dalfen Industrial affiliate for $21.3 million. The property, built in 1973 on 3.4 acres, is 100 percent leased to AerSale and generated an 11.1 percent unleveraged IRR. The sale price nearly doubled from the 2012 purchase price of $12.1 million.
stories.impact: Signals tight industrial supply and strong lease demand in Miami-Dade West (airport corridor). Developers should note that warehouse scarcity may be moderating near-term multifamily absorption (land-intensive logistics competes for limited developable acreage), but robust industrial pricing suggests healthy employment and logistics demand in metro Miami, supporting downstream residential inflow. Watch for pipeline backfill as developers compete for remaining industrial-zoned land near 826 and 836 corridors.

stories.title: Dwight Investment Management Supplies $115M Refi on Charlotte Apartments
stories.excerpt: Dwight Investment Management, an affiliate of Dwight Capital, closed the loan for the Seventeen Hundred on East property that opened in January with 295 luxury apartments and 6,500 square feet of retail space. Loan proceeds were used to retire existing construction debt, fund an interest reserve and provide cash-out proceeds, according to Dwight. Josh Hoffman, managing director at Dwight Investment Management, originated the loan. Located at 1755 Lombardy Circle in Charlotte’s Dilworth neighborhood, the property features a unit mix of eight studios, 158 one-bedroom units, 90 two-bedroom units and 39 three-bedroom units. Community amenities include a fitness center, a rooftop pool, coworking suites and a sky lounge. The retail portion of Seventeen Hundred on East has space for three ground-floor tenants that currently feature a Pilates studio, a Pvolve fitness club and the Om Spa. A food retailer is also planned. The Charlotte deal marks the second North Carolina financing from Dwight in less than a year. The private lender also provided a $42.5 million construction loan in October 2025 to Golden Hour Collective for its development of a 133-unit build-to-rent townhome community in Asheville, N.C., CO first reported at the time. Phillips Collective, a family office founded by Brian Phillips and Brittani Rotunda Phillips, did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Dwight Investment Management closes $115M refi on Seventeen Hundred on East, Charlotte, opened January 2025.
295 luxury apartments + 6,500 sq. ft. retail; construction loan repaid, interest reserve funded; Dilworth location.
Successful lease-up and refi signal strong Charlotte multifamily demand and lender appetite for Class A product.
stories.summary: Dwight Investment Management closed a $115 million refinance on Seventeen Hundred on East in Charlotte's Dilworth neighborhood, a 295-unit luxury apartment community with 6,500 sq. ft. of retail that opened in January 2025. Loan proceeds retired construction debt, funded interest reserves, and provided cash-out. The property features eight studios, 158 one-bedrooms, 90 two-bedrooms, and 39 three-bedrooms, plus fitness, rooftop pool, and coworking amenities.
stories.impact: Strong signal of Charlotte multifamily fundamentals; rapid stabilization and refi-ready performance by Q1 2025 indicates robust rental demand and pricing power in gateway neighborhoods like Dilworth. Charlotte's cost of living advantage (vs. coastal markets) and tech job growth (Bank of America, Lowe's, Truist) continue to attract in-migration. Developers should prioritize infill, transit-adjacent, and mixed-use sites in similar neighborhoods; lender appetite is present for Class A, reducing refinance risk and supporting higher basis underwriting.

stories.title: NIC MAP Sees $1T Gap Between Senior Housing Demand and Construction
stories.excerpt: The supply-demand imbalance in U.S. senior housing creates a $1-trillion investment opportunity, NIC MAP reported. NIC MAP’s updated Senior Housing Market Outlook shows that the nation’s 80+ population is entering a period of historic growth just as existing communities are filling up and new construction remains near historically low levels. With the first Baby Boomers turning 80 throughout 2026, the U.S. population age 80 and older is projected to grow by approximately one-third by 2030 and nearly double by 2040, adding roughly five million people within five years and 13 million within 15 years. Meanwhile, occupancy nationwide exceeds 90%, while construction starts have declined by roughly 67% since 2021. “Demographics on paper are increasingly becoming move-ins on the ground,” said Arick Morton, CEO of NIC MAP. “For operators, owners and capital providers, that is an important distinction. The question is no longer simply whether demand will arrive, but what the industry is doing to ensure that it will have sufficient capacity to serve it.” The post NIC MAP Sees $1T Gap Between Senior Housing Demand and Construction appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NIC MAP identifies $1T senior housing supply-demand gap; 80+ population grows 33% by 2030, 100% by 2040.
Construction starts down 67% since 2021; national occupancy exceeds 90%; first Baby Boomers turn 80 in 2026.
Historic demographic wave entering 2026; senior housing underbuilding creates multi-decade runway for development.
stories.summary: NIC MAP's Senior Housing Market Outlook highlights a critical supply-demand imbalance worth approximately $1 trillion. The U.S. population age 80 and older will grow by roughly one-third by 2030 (adding ~5 million people) and nearly double by 2040 (adding ~13 million), coinciding with national senior housing occupancy exceeding 90 percent and construction starts down 67 percent since 2021.
stories.impact: Urgent signal for diversified developers: senior housing represents the most undersupplied and fastest-growing demographic segment through 2045. Unlike multifamily, senior housing (independent living, assisted living, memory care) faces structural supply deficit, not cycle-driven oversupply. Capital should flow into senior housing development, partnering with operators and health systems; favorable reimbursement/occupancy dynamics and long-term demographic tailwinds mitigate lease-up risk. This is a multi-decade growth vector; delays in zoning and entitlements should be addressed now as demand is beginning to materialize.

stories.title: Namdar Group Lands $390M Construction Loan in Jersey City
stories.excerpt: Namdar Group has scored $390 million in construction financing for Park Tower, a 47-story multifamily project in the Journal Square neighborhood of Jersey City, NJ. Walker & Dunlop Capital Markets Institutional Advisory arranged the financing package, which includes a floating-rate, interest-only senior construction loan from Affinius Capital provided and a floating-rate, interest-only mezzanine loan from BH3 Fund Advisors. Located at 629 Newark Ave., Park Tower is slated for completion by May 2029. The Class A development will feature 1,049 residences, including 944 market-rate apartments and 105 affordable apartments. The half-million-square-foot property will also house 30 extended-stay hotel units and ground-floor retail just a five-minute walk from the Journal Square PATH station. Namdar Group, a privately owned real estate investment and development firm based in Great Neck, NY, focuses on large-scale transit-oriented developments in the U.S. and the Caribbean. The company currently has over 10,000 residential units in the approval and development process, according to its website. Namdar Group has collaborated with Walker & Dunlop on other projects in Journal Square. Walker & Dunlop arranged a $220 million refinancing for the developer’s 576-unit multifamily property 626 Newark Ave. in September 2025, followed by $180 million in financing for the 564-unit 35 Cottage St. in July of this year. The post Namdar Group Lands $390M Construction Loan in Jersey City appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Namdar Group secures $390M construction financing for Park Tower, Jersey City, 1,049 units, 47-story, completion May 2029.
944 market-rate + 105 affordable apartments; 30 extended-stay hotel units; 5-min walk to Journal Square PATH station.
Senior (Affinius Capital) + mezzanine (BH3 Fund Advisors) structure; Walker & Dunlop arranging; Namdar active in Jersey City transit deals.
stories.summary: Namdar Group closed $390 million in construction financing for Park Tower, a 47-story, 1,049-unit multifamily development in Jersey City's Journal Square neighborhood, expected to complete by May 2029. The project includes 944 market-rate apartments, 105 affordable units, 30 extended-stay hotel rooms, and ground-floor retail, all within a five-minute walk of the Journal Square PATH station. Financing combines a floating-rate senior loan from Affinius Capital and mezzanine from BH3 Fund Advisors.
stories.impact: Jersey City Journal Square remains a focused growth node for transit-oriented, mixed-use development. Successful construction financing on a >1,000-unit project signals lender confidence in NJ multifamily fundamentals and PATH corridor demand. Namdar's demonstrated track record (10,000+ units in pipeline) and repeated capital partnerships (multiple projects with Walker & Dunlop) validate Jersey City's desirability for NYC-proximate workforce. Developers should prioritize PATH-adjacent infill sites and mixed-income (market-rate + affordable) strategies; construction financing availability remains favorable for transit-anchored, large-scale projects in this submarket.

stories.title: Reforming Pilates to Open New Studio at 233 East 34th Street in Murray Hill
stories.excerpt: Almost started this story with a workout pun, but that would have been too much of a stretch. Fitness brand Reforming Pilates, which offers reformer equipment classes and heated mat workouts, has signed a 10-year, 2,500-square-foot lease to open a new location at 233 East 34th Street, according to landlord broker Meridian Capital Group. “Murray Hill is the heartbeat of Manhattan,” Genevieve Ross, founder of Reforming Pilates, said in a statement. “It’s where you move after college, where you find your people, and where New York really starts to feel like home. It’s young, it’s fun, and it was once my own playground. For me, opening here feels full circle — and I truly believe it’s one of the hottest places to be a brand in the city right now.” The deal represents the studio’s third Manhattan location, following spots at 109 West 17th Street in the Flatiron District and at 1305 Second Avenue on the Upper East Side. The asking rent for this deal was not disclosed, but the average asking rent for retail space in Manhattan’s nearby Herald Square neighborhood was $394 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE data. The landlord was represented in the deal by Meridian’s Noam Aziz, Carson Shahrabani and Max Freudenberger. “Murray Hill is evolving into a much more health-conscious and wellness-driven customer base,” Freudenberger said in a statement. “There is a growing demand for Pilates, fitness, wellness and health-focused concepts, and we believe this shift is creating a strong opportunity for operators that cater to today’s increasingly health-conscious consumer.” The South Florida-based Reforming Pilates was represented by Jeff Jacobson from Masonre. “We were not looking for another box,” Jacobson said in a statement. “Reforming Pilates needed a ground-floor studio in Murray Hill that could sit next to the Upper East Side and the Flatiron townhouse without dropping the standard — visible, purpose-built, 10 years.” Reforming Pilat
bullets: Reforming Pilates signs 10-year, 2,500 sq. ft. lease at 233 East 34th Street, Murray Hill, Manhattan.
Third Manhattan location (Flatiron, Upper East Side); fitness tenant signals continued retail vibrancy in residential neighborhoods.
Minimal relevance to multifamily supply/demand; represents retail leasing activity in strong residential submarket.
stories.summary: Reforming Pilates, a reformer and heated mat fitness brand, signed a 10-year lease for 2,500 sq. ft. at 233 East 34th Street in Murray Hill, Manhattan. This is the fitness studio's third Manhattan location, following openings in Flatiron and the Upper East Side. Asking rent was not disclosed, but the deal reflects strong retail tenant demand in the neighborhood.
stories.impact: Indirect positive signal: Murray Hill remains an attractive, amenity-rich residential neighborhood attracting experiential retail (fitness, wellness). This confirms continued renter demand for walkable, service-rich neighborhoods in Midtown East. However, the lease itself does not change multifamily supply/demand dynamics. Developers building or planning residential projects in similar neighborhoods should prioritize ground-floor retail/experiential space; fitness and wellness are premium lease drivers in young, urban-focused populations.

stories.title: Proptech Unicorn EliseAI Launches AI Agent Apollo
stories.excerpt: EliseAI, a leading artificial intelligence company automating housing and health care facilities and one of the first proptech firms to be valued at $1 billion, announced Thursday that it has launched Apollo, its first cross-platform agentic AI tool. A single AI agent capable of performing any task on the Elise platform, Apollo is designed as a new user interface for leasing agents, executives and others in property operations, according to the company. “Apollo is native to our platform, so anything you can do on the Elise AI platform, you can do with Apollo,” said Francesca Loftus, chief experience officer at Manhattan-based EliseAI. “It can execute requests as well as give you access to data across the entire system. A leasing agent would be able to say, ‘Send an updated message for everybody who toured yesterday,’ and be able to provide a message that gets sent out automatically through Apollo across everybody who fits those requirements.” Apollo can also provide next steps based on users’ questions “in plain language, both text and verbal,” Loftus added. Among Apollo’s functions are knowing a customer’s setup, as it understands every setting, permission and data definition specific to a team’s properties. EliseAI said Apollo acts at scale and has been tested against real operations, having run through thousands of tests covering everyday scenarios, from onboarding a new team member to first leasing inquiries, maintenance emergencies, and renewal conversations. It also inherits each user’s existing permissions, so it sees and does only what that person is already cleared for. “Every property team already has a dozen dashboards and reports telling them what happened,” Minna Song, co-founder and CEO of EliseAI, said in a statement. “[Apollo] already knows a team’s data, permissions and priorities well enough that people can ask it a question in plain English, get a real answer back, and see something actually happen because of it
bullets: EliseAI ($1B proptech unicorn) launches Apollo, cross-platform AI agent for leasing, property ops automation.
AI interface for leasing agents and executives; executes plain-language requests, tenant outreach, data aggregation.
Proptech innovation; immaterial to near-term supply/demand/capital/cost for apartment development; operational efficiency play.
stories.summary: EliseAI, a $1 billion proptech unicorn, announced Apollo, an agentic AI tool designed to automate leasing and property operations. Apollo operates natively on the EliseAI platform and executes tasks via plain-language text or voice commands, enabling leasing agents to send bulk tenant messages, access cross-system data, and automate follow-ups. The tool targets leasing agents, executives, and property operations teams.
stories.impact: Minimal near-term relevance to development underwriting, capital formation, or cost structure. However, AI-driven property management and leasing automation may compress operating expense growth long-term (labor, marketing), supporting margin stability in lower-growth cycles. Developers should monitor proptech adoption as a hedge against operator wage/cost inflation, but this tool does not change asset valuation, financing, or demand fundamentals today.
